messages.author: a5679449d442e116
messages.subject: Hybrid continuous/discrete faceted axes
parts:
I work in genetics, and have been making plots using ggplot2 that plot
association values or expression levels on the y-axis with genetic
position on the x axis.

I have been struggling for a while on how to annotate these plots with
information that also varies along the x-axis, such as the location of
genes, SNPs, etc.

It seemed to me that the "correct" way to do this would be to use a
shared x-axis, since all the various data I am plotting has this in
common, and the supported way to do that in ggplot2, as far as I can
tell, is to use faceting. I was able to use facet_grid to show two
different continuous variables, but when I tried to also show data
that has no continuous y-component but rather is categorical (such as
gene tracks), this resulted in various error messages (even when using
scales="free") and didn't work.

I can see how it might be difficult to implement this on the back-end,
but do you think it is a capability that might make sense to add? It
seems to me that it would be very useful to allow the concept of
"scale freedom" to extend beyond just having different limits on the
continuous scales to allow them to include discrete data as well.
Much of the annotation data we want to present alongside our results
looks like this, at least in my field, and it is very helpful to have
this annotation data presented in the same plot as, e.g. association
data, in order to better interpret the results.

In the meantime, I've had to kludge it by making up continuous values
for each discrete value and plotting them in the negative portion of
the y-axis, but having to do that breaks all kinds of things when it
comes to separating the data from the presentation, so it would be
really nice if some way to do this were supported within ggplot2.

An example of the sort of data I am working with is:
http://www.broadinstitute.org/files/shared/diabetes/scandinavs/chr9.jpg

Though in those plots they have also used two different continuous y-
axes in the same region of the plot, which I am now mostly convinced
is a bad idea because it is hard for the person viewing them not to
unintentionally compare the relative position of elements drawn on the
two different scales. In this case, that data can easily be displayed
using faceting in ggplot2 (with a free y-axis). The issue is the gene
track at the bottom that shows the location and direction of the genes
-- I can't find a clean way to present that information using ggplot2.

messages.author: b756a7daa2c2aa6d
messages.subject: Re: Hybrid continuous/discrete faceted axes
parts:
I agree that this would be a nice feature, but it's unlikely I'll ever
have the time to implement it - it would be a huge amount of effort
for something that isn't used all that often. An alternative that I
have thought a little about is a hybrid continuous/categorical scale -
this would be useful in your example, and in case where you have
different types of missing values you'd like to display along with the
non-missing data. The major hold up here is the lack of a built in R
data type to handle this sort of data.

Hadley

messages.subject: Re: Hybrid continuous/discrete faceted axes
parts:
Hi,
Just a thought here, even though the data is discrete, there is a
mapping to the continuous scale that the data is presented on. For
instance, if the position is chromosome 1, then that could be
transformed to position on the chromosome, say .5*length, so there is a
free parameter in the transformation. So couldn't one do something like
geom_anotatio() + scales(type =catTrans(alpha=.5)) or some such?
Maybe I am missing the point.

Hope this helps
Nicholas

messages.author: a5679449d442e116
messages.subject: Re: Hybrid continuous/discrete faceted axes
parts:
Hadley,

Thanks for consdering it -- I suspected it would not be an easy change
to add this to the faceting, though I do think that many users might
find it very useful (it certainly comes up in a large percentage of
the plots that I do). I agree that a hybrid scale would probably be
an easier way to solve it, but I see what you mean about not having a
data type in which you can put a mixed vector or factor/numeric types,
and I guess there probably isn't a lot of use for it in general.

Another way to solve the "problem" (in a less kludgey way than making
up fake continuous values for each of my discrete categories) would be
to make it easier to align scales across ggplot2 plots printed into
different viewports (basically making it possible to do "manual"
faceting).

This is already (sort of) possible by turning extra legends off and
forcing the scale limits to be the same, but it seems like there could
be a way to create an interface to make this easier, to make it work
even when there are extra elements (such as legends) in the margins.
I guess the problem with this is probably that the scale isn't
actually mapped to grid units until the plot is actually drawn, and
that data is (I am guessing) only contained in the grid objects.

Perhaps if we could create a new option for the scale functions that
would allow you to specify an existing ggplot2 viewport from which it
will copy all of its settings? Does that seem like something that
might be a bit easier to add? Is the necessary data currently stored
in the grid objects?

Josh.
